Eric Livshiz, Jake Vurpillat, Dylan Crookes, Tanveer Singh, Samuel Erlikhman

2026-06-08

Introduction

We live in the age of streaming services. In the U.S., Netflix, Prime Video, and Disney+ are the most popular, with many households often having many subscriptions. (https://www.statista.com/chart/25382/most-used-video-streaming-platforms/?srsltid=AfmBOoox1XeLW3YlbDt9wzhbtbIxPH0Cxz3AqZt9FTke_DGyZl5rTXjR). While it’s nice to have options, users may start to feel choice overload with the amount of content to choose from; having too many options can result in no choice. So, a user may spend time scrolling endlessly, with no result (at least we do). So, we thought of a question which many have been thought of before; can we use data to recommend movies that better match a user’s preferences?

This project utilizes recommender systems, as well as natural language processing (NLP). The recommender system is used for finding patterns within the data, and suggest similar films based on common features (i.e., a Star Wars IV query may return other Star Wars films, or Indiana Jones due to Harrison Ford starring in both, or Jurassic Park, due to John Williams composing the score of both films). Regarding NLP, a few of the features that define similarity and we intend to use are stored in text format (key plot words as an example). We can of course parse the list and analyze the words individually, but we want to preserve structural representations (think of all the famous movie quotes which will lose meaning otherwise!). We also aim to build an NLP-based chat interface, which allows the user to input a natural query (i.e., “recommend me a movie similar to Top Gun”), and receive a useful output.

Goal

We want to answer the following question: “Can we accurately recommend movies given film metadata, such as genre, keywords, cast, and other relevant features?”, using recommender systems and NLP, as well as to create a user interface to interact with our model

Data

We are lucky that we are not the only ones who care about statistics and films! There exists plenty of datasets regarding films, and we have chosen to use The Movies Dataset from Kaggle, as it contains data for ~45,000 films (we use “film” and “movie” interchangeably throughout this write-up, and want to point this out here to avoid any confusion, let’s hope our model believes there is no difference in these terms as well). The data is collected from MovieLens, a massive dataset which we will not be using, as it contains 33 million ratings and 86,000 movies, and is not reliant for research, and the details, credits, and keywords are taken from TMDB API. The dataset contains structured and unstructured data, and we will focus on the following files included:

  • movies_metadata.csv - overall movie information, i.e., title and genre
  • keywords.csv - quite useful, as it contains plot-related keywords which are stored as JSON objects
  • credits.csv - self-explanatory; the information about cast and crew
  • links.csv - mapping between the MovieLens, TMDB, and IMDB identifiers

The dataset includes two more CSVs, links_small.csv and ratings_small.csv, which are a subset of 9,000 movies - we want to work with the larger dataset to be more accurate, and we are not sure how the subset was selected (we are not sure if it is random, the first 9,000, or what algorithm what used to select the subset). It is important to note, that this dataset was last updated in 2017, meaning our dataset is missing thousands of recent movies. Looking at the above example, a natural similar film to Top Gun would be Top Gun: Maverick, which came out in 2022, but our system would fail to recommend it.

Methodology

We’d like to introduce how we will build our recommendation and NLP systems.

Recommendation System

This project stems from a content-based recommender systems, meaning that movies are recommended based on their similarity to other movies. This “similarity” is taken from film characteristics, i.e., genre and cast. We will implement this idea by making each movie a feature vector based on its attributes, we will use a similarity measure to be able to compare the movies, compute similarity score, and output the best n options. This can be achieved by using cosine similarity, where \(cos(\theta) = \frac{A \cdot B}{||A|| ||B||}\) . We measure the angle between two feature vectors, where \(A\) and \(B\) are two movies. The numerator is the dot product, meaning the overlap of the films’ features, and the denominator normalizes given the length of vector. The resulting value is from -1 to 1; -1 means that the films are absolute opposites, whereas 1 means that the movies are almost identical (think Mission Impossible films). Cosine similarity is quite useful in our context as it focuses on feature patterns, rather than the scale.

NLP

Natural language processing is used in this project to understand text-based movie features, as well as for user interaction. As previously mentioned, the keywords and cast lists are stored in a text format and are not easily interpreted by a computer. One way to deal with this data is to find the most useful text-based features (genre and keyword, versus studio or release date). We merge these features into a text representation for each movie (which is referred to as a bag of words), and convert the text to numerical representation using the Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) method. This process assigns weights to words based on how important it is to the entire dataset \(TF-IDF(t, d) = TF(t, d) \cdot log(\frac{N}{DF(t)})\). We can then feed natural sentences to a chatbot, have it process the query, and formulate it into a proper query to the recommender system. Let’s go ahead and get started with the data cleaning.

Merging

Let’s now go ahead and merge datasets. We see the following mapping: movies\(id = tmdbId keywords\)id = tmdbId credits\(id = tmdbId ratings\)movieId = MovieLens Id

Links does not have IDs, but the order in which the movies are stored is the same order as the the movie metadata dataset. Let’s merge movies, keywords, and credits by tmdbId, map ratings’ movieId to tmdbId using links, summarize ratings by movie, and merge rating summaries into the full data.

movies_full <- merge_movies_keywords_credits(movies_clean, keywords, credits)

ratings_join_out <- map_ratings_to_tmdb_summaries(ratings_clean, links)
ratings_mapped <- ratings_join_out$ratings_mapped
ratings_summary <- ratings_join_out$ratings_summary

movies_final <- join_rating_summaries(movies_full, ratings_summary)

Distribution of Ratings

This is expected; users seem to be more likely to either give a “slightly above average” rating, or a complete dislike, i,e, 0. Few usually give full marks. So the data is slightly skewed to the left.

Ratings Count

We see a long tail, with the data skewed to the right. This again, does make sense - most films don’t receive many ratings. The Modeling

Now with all the data cleaning and visualizations we have seen above, its now time to get into the most important part of this process, building the NLP and Recommender models.

NLP Model

Recommender Model

Preparing for recommender

The last thing we need to do is prepare the NLP for the recommender, so we will create a feature matrix, where we take the tf_idfs and assign them a value based on the movie they are most related to.

Each column represents a bigram feature, each cell contains TF-IDF weight for that bigram in that movie.

movies_feature_matrix <- create_feature_matrix(bigram_tf_idf_clean)

Here, we create a lookup table with the metadata required for recommendations. Converts the feature matrix into a sparse matrix and lines up the lookup table with the feature matrix row-wise to match movie IDs.

prepared <- prepare_movie_search(movies_text, movies_feature_matrix)

movie_search <- prepared$movie_search
movies_feature_matrix <- prepared$movies_feature_matrix

dim(movies_feature_matrix)
## [1] 41548 21344

Identifies sparsity in the recommender feature matrix, helping us identify zero values.

create_recommender_summary(movies_feature_matrix)
Sparse Feature Matrix Summary
movies features nonzero_values sparsity
41548 21344 173599 0.9998

We now create two functions;one that rescales numeric variables to values between 0 and 1 in order to achieve parity across variables, as well as one that deals with cosine similarity. The function calculates vectors for each movie to be used in comparison against other movies in the feature matrix.

movie_row_norms <- matrix_row_norms(movies_feature_matrix)

similarities <- cosine_against_one_movie(
  movie_id = "862",
  feature_matrix = movies_feature_matrix,
  row_norms = movie_row_norms
)

head(similarities)
##  2  3  5  6 11 12 
##  0  0  0  0  0  0

Finds the movie ID associated with a user’s query using a multitude of methods, prioritizing more well known and highly rated movies in case of duplicates.

find_movie_id <- function(title_query, movie_lookup) {
  title_query_clean <- str_to_lower(str_squish(title_query))
  
  exact_match <- movie_lookup %>%
    filter(str_to_lower(title) == title_query_clean) %>%
    arrange(desc(tmdb_popularity), desc(tmdb_vote_average))
  
  if (nrow(exact_match) > 0) {
    return(exact_match$id[1])
  }
  
  partial_match <- movie_lookup %>%
    filter(str_detect(str_to_lower(title), fixed(title_query_clean))) %>%
    arrange(desc(tmdb_popularity), desc(tmdb_vote_average))
  
  if (nrow(partial_match) > 0) {
    return(partial_match$id[1])
  }
  
  stop("No matching movie title was found. Try a simpler or more exact title.")
}

Given a movie title, finds similar movies using TF-IDF cosine similarity then ranks them using a score combining content similarity as well as adding weights to popularity and rating to achieve more accurate ratings.

results <- recommend_similar_movies("Toy Story", n = 10)
results$input_movie
results$recommendations

Natural Language Query Recommender

Here we prepare natural language queries for the recommender. We do this by converting queries into bigrams, applying the same IDF weights used for movie text, and return a sparse query vector.

bigram_idf_lookup <- bigram_tf_idf_clean %>%
  distinct(bigram, idf) %>%
  mutate(bigram = as.character(bigram))

Here we have the main NLP recommender with a hybrid approach bridging popularity and rating with the similarity score returned from the NLP.

Overall, the final recommendation given by the NLP utilizes a hybridized approach incorporating a movie’s popularity as well as its rating rather than just pure text sumilarity. We convert the query into a TF-IDF vector and compare it with each movie using cosine similarity. We then rank the most similar movies in order, descending and return a list.

Conclusion

We live in the age of streaming, where platforms like Netflix and Prime Video offer tens of thousands of titles, yet users frequently encounter choice overload, resulting in endless scrolling without selection. In this project, we designed and built a content-based movie recommendation system that leverages both structured film metadata and natural language processing (NLP). Using The Movies Dataset from Kaggle (~45,000 films with metadata sourced from TMDB and MovieLens), we performed data cleaning and exploratory data analysis to isolate meaningful features, accounting for structural elements like cast, crew, genres, and text-based plot overviews.

To translate raw text into machine-readable representations, we utilized tokenization and TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) calculations. By extracting bigrams (such as “Sci-Fi” or “World War II”) from the text data, we preserved the contextual, structural representation of movie descriptions. This allowed us to build a comprehensive feature matrix for computing cosine similarity between feature vectors. Crucially, our testing confirmed that a pure text-similarity model occasionally surfaces obscure, low-quality outliers that happen to share high keyword overlap. We introduce a hybrid scoring algorithm, which balances content similarity with weighted TMDB popularity and average user ratings which substantially improved recommendation quality.

However, several distinct limitations remain. Because our dataset caps off in July 2017, the system is blind to recent cinematic releases, preventing natural recommendations like modern sequels. Furthermore, as a strict content-based system, it operates without historical user profile data, limiting its capacity for personalized collaborative filtering. The project is also strictly Bigram related; it can tell if two words are related, and has no clue about culture relevance or cinematic universes, it only recommends films that have similar word structure. Finally, the weights used in our hybrid scoring system were tuned experimentally rather than via formal cross-validation or optimization.

Future iterations could resolve these limitations by integrating a live data pipeline via the TMDB API, layering in user-level collaborative filtering to build a true hybrid recommender, or utilizing a transformer-based language model to parse more complex or ambiguous user queries. Ultimately, this project demonstrates that even without deep learning architectures, a well-engineered pipeline that is grounded in meticulous data cleaning, thoughtful feature extraction, and a balanced hybrid ranking strategy can produce a highly practical and effective movie recommendation system.
